Neonatal domestic horses, or foals, typically emerge with a wet weight at birth of approximately 38,000 grams [Wwb = approximately 38,000 grams], representing a substantial investment by the mare relative to her own ultimate wet weight and reflecting the precocial developmental strategy characteristic of the genus Equus. This high initial mass, which can approach 10% of the maternal adult body mass, facilitates rapid locomotor development, enabling the neonate to follow the herd within hours of parturition. The exceptional mass at birth is accompanied by a relatively long gestation period, which reflects the extended time required for in utero organogenesis and musculoskeletal maturation. In the domestic horse, gestation time has been recorded at 337 days [tg = 337 days] when the mare is maintained at a core body temperature of 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C], a value arising from thermoregulatory constraints during foetal development. This duration is among the longest observed in domestic ungulates and is a critical determinant of the species' life-history pace, as a single, large, well-developed foal is produced per litter, limiting maximum annual reproductive output.

The lactation-dependent nursing phase that follows parturition constitutes a period of rapid growth and profound physiological transition for the suckling juvenile. Weaning, defined as the cessation of suckling and the onset of nutritional independence, occurs at a time since birth at weaning of 730 days [tx = 730 days] under standard husbandry conditions at 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C]. This relatively late weaning age, which significantly exceeds the 30 to 35 days frequently cited as the minimum for voluntary solid food intake, reflects the protracted period of maternal milk provisioning required to support the foal's accelerated skeletal and muscular growth trajectory. During this pre-weaning interval, the neonate more than doubles its birth mass, gradually transitioning from a diet composed exclusively of milk to one incorporating forage. The extended period of maternal dependence is a key life-history feature, as it ensures that the growing individual accumulates sufficient energy reserves before facing the metabolic demands of a fully herbivorous diet and the social pressures of herd integration.

Under the thermal conditions typical of the species' active metabolic state, which is defined by a core body temperature of 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C], the process of sexual maturation unfolds at markedly different rates between the sexes. Fillies achieve puberty at a time since birth at puberty for female of 914 days [tp = 914 days], whereas colts require a significantly longer period, reaching puberty at 973 days since birth [tp = 973 days since birth]. at a temp at a temperature of 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C]erature of 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C]This sex-specific divergence in maturational timing is a common pattern among polygynous equids, where males benefit from continued somatic growth to improve their competitive ability for access to receptive females. During this post-weaning, pre-reproductive juvenile stage, sub-adult individuals continue to refine their foraging skills and establish dominance hierarchies within the herd. The onset of gonadal activity marks the transition from the immature organism to the reproductively viable adult, though social and ecological factors may further delay the age at first successful mating.

The domestic horse exhibits one of the most extended life spans among domesticated eutherian mammals, with a maximum recorded longevity of 20,805 days [am = 20,805 days] at a typical core body temperature of 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C], a value equivalent to approximately 57 years. This exceptional longevity is a consequence of a slow life-history pace, characterized by a single, high-investment foal per reproductive event and a prolonged period of parental care. The species' slow somatic senescence is supported by a robust physiological capacity for tissue maintenance, low extrinsic mortality rates in managed populations, and a digestive system adapted to processing fibrous plant material efficiently over many decades. In terms of adult body size, which is a key correlate of lifespan among large herbivores, the ultimate wet weight of the domestic horse reaches approximately 450,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 450,000 grams], although the Animal Diversity Web reports a broader range extending from 227,000 to 900,000 grams depending on breed and management. This substantial adult mass places the horse among the largest extant terrestrial mammals, and it is a primary factor underlying its slow reproductive turnover and extended life span.

The reproductive strategy of the domestic horse is characterized by extremely low fecundity, as each litter consists of a single foal [N_R_i = each litter consists of a single foal], produced at a slow interval that yields a maximum reproduction frequency of one litter every 548 days [F_R_i = one litter every 548 days] at a core body temperature of 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C]. This low rate of offspring production, among the lowest recorded for any ungulate, is a direct consequence of the exceptionally long gestation period and the extended lactation-dependent nursing phase that delays the resumption of ovarian cyclicity in the dam. It is important to contextualize the horse's adult body mass relative to this reproductive output; an adult female can attain an ultimate wet weight of up to 450,000 grams [Wwi = up to 450,000 grams], as reported in standard breed surveys. The combination of a massive, precocial neonate, a long inter-birth interval, and a pronounced sex-specific difference in the timing of puberty underscores the horse's position as an extreme K-selected strategist within the mammalian order Perissodactyla, a pattern that is reflected in its extended life span and low annual reproductive rate.
